questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain three components of a transaction processing system (TPS). (3 marks)

(b) Give two limitations of TPS compared to Management Information System. (2 marks)

(c) State the purpose and the expected goal of a school information system. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Components of a TPS (3 marks - any three)**

A transaction processing system records and processes the routine day-to-day transactions of an organisation (sales, payments, enrolments, bookings...). Its main components are:

1. **Input (data capture).** The transaction data are collected at the moment the transaction happens, from source documents or directly by devices such as keyboards, barcode readers, point-of-sale terminals or ATMs. The data are checked (validated) as they enter.
2. **Processing.** The software and the processor carry out the standard operations on each transaction: calculate, sort, classify and update. Processing is done in batch mode (transactions collected and processed together, e.g. payroll) or in real-time/online mode (each transaction processed at once, e.g. a bank withdrawal).
3. **Storage (database / files).** The master files and transaction files hold the records (customers, stock, accounts). They are updated after each transaction so that they always reflect the current position.
4. **Output.** The results are produced as receipts, invoices, statements, pay slips and confirmation messages, and as routine reports for the operational staff.

(The users and the procedures that govern how transactions are handled are sometimes counted as further components.)

**(b) Two limitations of a TPS compared with an MIS (2 marks)**

- A TPS only **records and processes routine, detailed data**; it does not summarise them into **management reports** (trends, comparisons, exceptions) for tactical decisions, whereas an MIS turns the TPS data into summary information for middle managers.
- A TPS serves the **operational level** only and has **no analysis or decision-support capability** (no forecasting, no 'what-if' analysis, no strategic view of the whole organisation), whereas an MIS draws on data from several departments to support planning and control.

(Other acceptable points: the output of a TPS is mostly detailed and fixed in format, and a TPS is not designed to combine data from different sources.)

**(c) School information system (3 marks)**

- **Purpose.** To collect, store, process and distribute the data of the school (students' records, attendance, marks and report cards, staff, timetables, fees and accounts, library and stock) so that teachers, administrators and parents can obtain accurate information when they need it.
- **Expected goal.** To make the management of the school **more efficient and accurate**: less paperwork and fewer errors, quick access to reliable information, better communication with parents, and better decisions (for example on class sizes, resources or students who need support), which finally improves the quality of teaching and of the results.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Give two characteristics of each of impact printer and laser printer. (2 marks)

(b) Give one advantage of each of the printers above. (2 marks)

(c) Name another type of printer. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Characteristics (2 marks)**

| Impact printer (e.g. dot-matrix) | Laser printer |
|---|---|
| It forms the characters by **striking an inked ribbon against the paper** with pins or hammers (physical contact). | It is a **non-impact** printer: a laser beam draws the page image on a charged drum, toner sticks to it and is fused onto the paper by heat. |
| It is **noisy** and relatively **slow**, and the print quality is low (visible dots). | It prints **a whole page at a time**, quickly and quietly, at high resolution. |

**(b) One advantage of each (2 marks)**

- **Impact printer:** it can print **carbon copies / multi-part stationery** in one pass (invoices, receipts), and its ribbon and paper are cheap and it works in dusty or hot places.
- **Laser printer:** it gives **high-quality, sharp text and graphics at high speed**, with a low cost per page for large print runs.

**(c) Another type of printer (1 mark)**

The **inkjet (bubble-jet) printer**, which sprays tiny drops of liquid ink onto the paper. (Other correct answers: thermal printer, line printer, plotter, 3D printer.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Give one characteristic of each of 1st Generation and 3rd Generation computers. (2 marks)

(b) State and describe what two characteristics determine the power of a laptop (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Computer generations (2 marks)**

- **First generation (about 1940-1956):** the computers used **vacuum tubes** as electronic switches. They were very large, expensive, consumed much power, produced a lot of heat and broke down often; they were programmed in machine language, with punched cards for input.
- **Third generation (about 1964-1971):** the computers used **integrated circuits (ICs)**, i.e. many transistors on a small silicon chip. They were much smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable than the earlier ones; they introduced keyboards and monitors, operating systems and high-level languages.

(One characteristic of each is enough for the mark.)

**(b) Two characteristics that determine the power of a laptop (2 marks)**

1. **Processor (CPU) speed and type.** The clock speed in GHz and the number of cores (and the cache size) set how many instructions the laptop executes each second: a faster processor with more cores runs programs and several tasks at once more quickly.
2. **Size of RAM (main memory).** RAM holds the programs and data in use. With more RAM (for example 16 GB instead of 4 GB) more applications can be open at the same time without the system swapping data to the slower disk, so the laptop stays fast.

(Other accepted answers: type and speed of the storage (SSD faster than hard disk), graphics card.)
